sk: अथ हैनं सौर्यायणी गार्ग्यः पप्रच्छ भगवन्नेतस्मिन्पुरुषे कानि स्वपन्ति कान्यस्मिञ्जाग्रति कतर एष देवः स्वप्नान्पश्यति कस्यैतत्सुखं भवति कस्मिन्नु सर्वे सम्प्रतिष्ठिता भवन्तीति ||
ro: atha · ha · enaṁ · sauryāyaṇī · gārgyaḥ · papraccha · bhagavan · etasmin · puruṣe · kāni · svapanti · kāni · asmin · jāgrati · kataraḥ · eṣaḥ · devaḥ · svapnān · paśyati · kasya · etat · sukhaṁ · bhavati · kasmin · nu · sarve · sampratiṣṭhitāḥ · bhavanti · iti ||
hi: तब सौर्यायणी गार्ग्य ने (पिप्पलाद से) पूछा — 'भगवन्! इस पुरुष (मनुष्य) में कौन-कौन (देव/शक्तियाँ) सोते हैं? कौन-कौन इसमें जागते हैं? कौन-सा देव स्वप्न (सपने) देखता है? यह सुख किसका होता है (सुषुप्ति का सुख किसे मिलता है)? और ये सब किसमें प्रतिष्ठित (स्थापित) होते हैं?'
en: Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya asked him: 'Bhagavan! In this person (puruṣa), which (faculties) sleep? Which remain awake? Which god (deva) sees dreams? Whose is this happiness (sukha, of deep sleep)? And in whom are all these established?'

ws.h: सोते हैं / निद्रा में चले जाते हैं

gr: Five sub-questions: (1) kāni svapanti — which faculties sleep? (2) kāni jāgrati — which remain awake? (3) kataraḥ devaḥ svapnān paśyati — which god sees dreams? (4) kasya etat sukham — whose is this happiness (of deep sleep)? (5) kasmin sarve sampratiṣṭhitāḥ — in whom are all established? The questions move from the observable (sleep/waking) to the philosophical (who is the dreamer? whose is the bliss? what is the ground?). Question 4 shifts from prāṇa-physiology (Questions 1-3) to psychology and consciousness-theory. kasya etat sukham — 'whose is this happiness?' is the most penetrating sub-question. In deep sleep, there are no objects, no senses, no thoughts — yet we wake refreshed and happy. If no 'experiencer' was present, who experienced the happiness? This question leads directly to the discovery of the Self as the witness of all three states.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह प्रश्न अवस्था-त्रय-विवेक (discrimination of three states) का है — जो अद्वैत वेदान्त का मूलभूत साधन है। जाग्रत, स्वप्न, सुषुप्ति — तीनों अवस्थाओं के साक्षी (witness) को पहचानना ही आत्मज्ञान है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this question concerns avasthā-traya-viveka (discrimination of the three states) — the fundamental method of Advaita Vedānta. Recognising the witness (sākṣī) of all three states — waking, dream, deep sleep — is Self-knowledge.
advaita.ins: You sleep, you dream, you wake. Three states, three different worlds. But you — the one who remembers all three — you never change. Finding that unchanging 'you' is the entire point of this question.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'कस्यैतत्सुखम्' — सुषुप्ति का सुख जीवात्मा का है, जो भगवान् के सान्निध्य (proximity) में विश्राम करता है। सुषुप्ति में जीव भगवान् के निकटतम होता है — इसीलिए सुख अनुभव होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'kasya etat sukham' — the happiness of deep sleep belongs to the jīvātman, which rests in the proximity of the Lord. In deep sleep, the jīva is closest to the Lord — hence the experience of happiness.
vishisht.ins: Why do you feel happy after deep sleep? Because in deep sleep, you were closest to God. No senses, no thoughts, no ego — just the soul resting near its source. That proximity is bliss.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — तीन अवस्थाएँ चेतना के तीन स्तर हैं: जाग्रत = बाह्य चेतना (surface consciousness), स्वप्न = अन्तर्चेतना (inner/subliminal consciousness), सुषुप्ति = अधिचेतन/अवचेतन (superconscient/subconscient) से सम्पर्क। 'कस्य सुखम्' — यह अधिचेतन आनन्द (superconscient bliss) की झलक है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the three states are three levels of consciousness: waking = surface consciousness, dream = inner/subliminal consciousness, deep sleep = contact with the superconscient/subconscient. 'Kasya sukham' — this is a glimpse of superconscient bliss.
aurobindo.ins: Waking shows you the surface. Dreams show you the depths. Deep sleep takes you beyond both — into a territory where thought can't follow. The happiness you bring back from there is a souvenir from the superconscient.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the happiness of deep sleep a philosophical problem?
dp.a: The happiness of deep sleep (suṣupti-sukha) is one of the deepest puzzles in Indian philosophy. The problem: (1) In deep sleep, the five senses are inactive. The mind is not producing thoughts. There is no object of perception, no desire, no memory. (2) Yet we wake from deep sleep and say: 'I slept well; I was happy; I knew nothing.' (3) This raises three questions: Who experienced the happiness? The senses were off, the mind was off — so who was the experiencer? What was the object of happiness? In waking, happiness comes from getting what you want. In deep sleep, there is no object — yet there is happiness. Who remembers? If the mind was asleep, who retains the memory 'I slept happily'? The Upanishadic answer is that a witness (sākṣī) was present throughout — the Ātman, which is svayam-prakāśa (self-luminous). The happiness of deep sleep is not caused by any external object but is the natural state of the Self — ānanda (bliss) uncontaminated by sensory activity. Māṇḍūkya 5 calls this state ānandabhuk ('bliss-enjoyer') and names the Self in this state prājña ('the wise one / the knower'). Shankara's Advaita uses this analysis as a key argument: if the Self's natural state (deep sleep) is blissful, then unhappiness is not natural but imposed by ignorance (avidyā). Remove the ignorance, and the ever-present bliss shines through.

dp.q: 🔍 The three states in Indian philosophy
dp.a: The avasthā-traya (three states of consciousness) analysis is foundational across Indian philosophical schools: (1) Jāgrat (waking): The senses are active, the mind processes external data, the ego identifies with the body. The Self is called Viśva (the Universal) or Vaiśvānara (the common-to-all-men) in this state (Māṇḍūkya 3). Consciousness is externalised. (2) Svapna (dream): The senses are withdrawn, but the mind remains active — it creates an entire world from memory-traces (vāsanās). The Self is called Taijasa (the Luminous) in this state (Māṇḍūkya 4). Consciousness is internalised. The dreamer is simultaneously the creator, perceiver, and material of the dream-world — a fact the Upanishads use as a model for understanding creation itself. (3) Suṣupti (deep sleep): Both senses and mind are withdrawn. There is no duality, no subject-object split, no desire. The Self is called Prājña (the Knower) in this state (Māṇḍūkya 5). Consciousness is unified — but veiled by ignorance (the sleeper doesn't know he is the Self). (4) Turīya (the Fourth): not a 'state' but the ground of all three states — the witness that is present in waking, dream, and deep sleep but is not limited to any of them. The Māṇḍūkya identifies this as Ātman = Brahman. Question 4 of the Prashna covers states 1-3; the answer to 'kasmin sarve sampratiṣṭhitāḥ' ('in whom are all established?') points toward the Fourth.

sk: तस्मै स होवाच यथा गार्ग्य मरीचयो ऽर्कस्यास्तं गच्छतः सर्वा एतस्मिंस्तेजोमण्डल एकीभवन्ति ताः पुनः पुनरुदयतः प्रचरन्त्येवं ह वै तत्सर्वं परे देवे मनस्येकीभवति तेन तर्ह्येष पुरुषो न शृणोति न पश्यति न जिघ्रति न रसयते न स्पृशते नाभिवदते नादत्ते नानन्दयते न विसृजते नेयायते स्वपितीत्याचक्षते ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · yathā · gārgya · marīcayaḥ · arkasya · astaṁ · gacchataḥ · sarvāḥ · etasmin · tejo-maṇḍale · ekībhavanti · tāḥ · punaḥ · punaḥ · udayataḥ · pracaranti · evaṁ · ha · vai · tat · sarvaṁ · pare · deve · manasi · ekībhavati · tena · tarhi · eṣaḥ · puruṣaḥ · na · śṛṇoti · na · paśyati · na · jighrati · na · rasayate · na · spṛśate · na · abhivadate · na · ādatte · na · ānandayate · na · visṛjate · na · iyāyate · svapiti · iti · ācakṣate ||
hi: उनसे उन्होंने (पिप्पलाद ने) कहा — 'हे गार्ग्य! जैसे अस्त होते हुए सूर्य (अर्क) की सब किरणें (मरीचयः) इस तेजोमण्डल (प्रकाश-वृत्त) में एकीभूत हो जाती हैं, और फिर उदय होने पर पुनः फैल जाती हैं — वैसे ही वह सब कुछ (सब इन्द्रियाँ) पर देव मन में एकीभूत हो जाता है। इसलिए तब यह पुरुष (मनुष्य) न सुनता है, न देखता है, न सूँघता है, न स्वाद लेता है, न स्पर्श करता है, न बोलता है, न ग्रहण करता है, न आनन्द लेता है, न उत्सर्जन करता है, न गमन करता है — (तब लोग) कहते हैं कि वह सो गया।'
en: To him he said: 'As, O Gārgya, the rays (marīci) of the setting sun all become one in that disc of light (tejo-maṇḍala), and spread forth again when it rises — so all (the senses) become one in the supreme god, the mind (manas). Therefore, this person then neither hears, nor sees, nor smells, nor tastes, nor touches, nor speaks, nor grasps, nor enjoys, nor excretes, nor moves about. They say: "He sleeps."'

ws.h: एक हो जाती हैं / विलीन हो जाती हैं

ws.e: in the supreme god, the mind

ws.h: सोता है / निद्रा में जाता है

gr: The sun-simile: at sunset, the sun's countless rays withdraw into its disc; at sunrise, they spread forth again. Sleep is the 'sunset' of the senses — all ten faculties (five jñānendriyas + five karmendriyas) merge into the mind. Waking is the 'sunrise'. pare deve manasi — 'in the supreme deity, the mind': the mind is called para deva (supreme god) not because it is the ultimate reality but because among the sensory faculties, the mind is the highest — it is the 'sun' from which all sense-functions radiate. Ten negations: na śṛṇoti, na paśyati, na jighrati, na rasayate, na spṛśate (five jñānendriyas cease) + na abhivadate, na ādatte, na ānandayate, na visṛjate, na iyāyate (five karmendriyas cease). This exhaustive list of ten cessations defines the state of sleep precisely: all faculties are withdrawn. svapiti iti ācakṣate — 'they say he sleeps': the folk-term 'sleep' is now given its technical meaning — the merging of all faculties into the mind.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सूर्य-किरण उपमा यह दिखाती है कि इन्द्रियाँ मन से पृथक (separate) नहीं — जैसे किरणें सूर्य से पृथक नहीं। निद्रा में किरणें लौटती हैं; जागरण में फैलती हैं। मन = 'पर देव' — इन्द्रियों में सर्वोच्च।
advaita.en: Shankara says the sun-ray simile shows the senses are not separate from the mind — as rays are not separate from the sun. In sleep, the rays return; in waking, they spread. Mind = 'para deva' — the highest among the faculties.
advaita.ins: Your five senses are not five independent workers. They're five rays of one sun — the mind. At night the sun sets, the rays disappear. They were never really separate. They were always the mind, reaching outward.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — निद्रा में इन्द्रियों का मन में विलय ईश्वर की योजना (divine design) है — शरीर को विश्राम (rest) देने के लिए। 'पर देव मनसि' — मन ईश्वर का प्रमुख आन्तरिक उपकरण (inner instrument) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the merging of senses into the mind during sleep is the Lord's design — to give the body rest. 'Para deva manasi' — the mind is the Lord's chief inner instrument.
vishisht.ins: Sleep isn't a failure of consciousness — it's planned maintenance. The Lord withdraws the senses into the mind every night so the body can repair itself. You think you chose to sleep. The Lord chose to service the machine.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — दस निषेध (ten negations) यह दिखाते हैं कि निद्रा में बाह्य चेतना (surface consciousness) पूर्णतः अन्तर्मुख (inward-turned) हो जाती है। किन्तु चेतना स्वयं विलुप्त नहीं होती — वह केवल बाह्य से आन्तरिक हो जाती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the ten negations show that in sleep, surface consciousness becomes completely inward-turned. But consciousness itself does not vanish — it merely shifts from external to internal.
aurobindo.ins: Sleep isn't unconsciousness — it's consciousness looking inward instead of outward. The ten senses shut their windows, and the mind turns to face the interior. What it sees there is the dream. What it rests in beyond the dream is the deep sleep.

dp.q: 🔍 The sun-ray simile for sleep
dp.a: The sun-ray simile (marīci-upamā) is one of the Prashna Upanishad's most vivid images. At sunset, the sun's countless individual rays merge back into the solar disc — they don't vanish but return to their source. At sunrise, they spread forth again, reaching every corner of the visible world. Sleep works identically: Sunset = falling asleep: the ten sense-faculties (five cognitive + five active) withdraw from their objects and merge into the mind. Just as the rays don't disappear (they're still 'in' the sun), the faculties don't vanish (they're still 'in' the mind). Sunrise = waking up: the faculties spread forth again from the mind, each resuming its function. Eyes see, ears hear, hands grasp — the rays reach out. The simile teaches three things: (1) Non-destruction: sleep doesn't destroy the senses; it absorbs them. This is why they return intact on waking. (2) Unity in source: all ten faculties originate from one mind, just as all rays originate from one sun. Diversity (ten senses) is an expansion of unity (one mind). (3) Cyclicity: the sleep-wake cycle mirrors the cosmic day-night cycle. The microcosm (person) recapitulates the macrocosm (sun) daily.

dp.q: 🔍 Why are ten faculties listed?
dp.a: The mantra lists ten cessations, corresponding to the ten indriyas of Sāṅkhya-Vedāntic psychology: Five jñānendriyas (cognitive senses): (1) na śṛṇoti — does not hear (śrotra / ear). (2) na paśyati — does not see (cakṣu / eye). (3) na jighrati — does not smell (ghrāṇa / nose). (4) na rasayate — does not taste (rasanā / tongue). (5) na spṛśate — does not touch (tvak / skin). Five karmendriyas (active faculties): (6) na abhivadate — does not speak (vāk / speech). (7) na ādatte — does not grasp (pāṇi / hand). (8) na ānandayate — does not enjoy sexually (upastha / reproductive organ). (9) na visṛjate — does not excrete (pāyu / excretory organ). (10) na iyāyate — does not move (pāda / feet). When all ten shut down, the person is 'asleep'. But something remains active — the prāṇa-fires, described in the next mantra. Sleep is therefore not total cessation but selective withdrawal: the senses sleep, but prāṇa stays awake.

sk: प्राणाग्नय एवैतस्मिन्पुरे जाग्रति गार्हपत्यो ह वा एषो ऽपानो व्यानो ऽन्वाहार्यपचनः ||
ro: prāṇa-agnayaḥ · eva · etasmin · pure · jāgrati · gārhapatyaḥ · ha · vā · eṣaḥ · apānaḥ · vyānaḥ · anvāhārya-pacanaḥ ||
hi: इस पुर (शरीर-नगर) में प्राणाग्नियाँ (प्राण-रूपी अग्नियाँ) ही जागती रहती हैं। गार्हपत्य अग्नि — वह यह अपान है। व्यान — वह अन्वाहार्यपचन (दक्षिणाग्नि) है।
en: The Prāṇa-fires alone remain awake in this city (pura, the body). The Gārhapatya fire — that is this apāna. The Anvāhāryapacana (Dakṣiṇāgni) fire — that is vyāna.

ws.h: गार्हपत्य अग्नि — गृहस्थ की मुख्य अग्नि

gr: The body as a sacrificial arena: this mantra introduces a remarkable metaphor — the three Vedic ritual fires are mapped onto three prāṇas: (1) Gārhapatya (householder's fire, western) = apāna; (2) Anvāhāryapacana/Dakṣiṇāgni (southern fire) = vyāna; (3) Āhavanīya (offering fire, eastern) = prāṇa (detailed in the next mantra). prāṇa-agnayaḥ jāgrati — 'the prāṇa-fires stay awake': while the ten senses merge into the mind during sleep, the prāṇas continue to function — the heart beats, digestion continues, blood circulates. The 'fires' never go out. pura — 'city': the body is called a 'city' (cf. 'pura' in 'puruṣa' — the one who dwells in the pura). This echoes the Kaṭha's 'city of eleven gates' (2.1.1) and the Bhagavad Gītā's 'city of nine gates' (5.13).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — इन्द्रियाँ सोती हैं, किन्तु प्राण-अग्नियाँ जागती रहती हैं — यह सिद्ध करता है कि प्राण इन्द्रियों से स्वतंत्र (independent) है। गार्हपत्य = अपान — क्योंकि गार्हपत्य मूल-अग्नि (source-fire) है, जिससे अन्य अग्नियाँ प्रज्वलित होती हैं; अपान भी मूल-प्राण है जो शरीर की नींव (foundation) बनाता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the senses sleep but the prāṇa-fires stay awake — proving that Prāṇa is independent of the senses. Gārhapatya = apāna because the Gārhapatya is the source-fire from which other fires are kindled; apāna is similarly the foundational prāṇa that supports the body's base functions.
advaita.ins: Ten workers go home at night. But three furnaces in the factory keep burning — if they go out, the factory is destroyed. Your senses sleep, but apāna, vyāna, and prāṇa never rest. Stop any one of them, and the body dies.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — शरीर को 'पुर' (नगर) कहना — यह ईश्वर के निवास-स्थान (temple) का सूचक है। प्राण-अग्नियाँ मंदिर की नित्य-ज्वाला (eternal flame) हैं — ईश्वर की उपस्थिति का प्रमाण।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says calling the body 'pura' (city) indicates it is the Lord's dwelling-place (temple). The prāṇa-fires are the temple's eternal flame — proof of the Lord's presence.
vishisht.ins: A temple's lamp never goes out. Similarly, the Lord keeps three fires burning in your body-temple — even while you sleep. Those fires are His signature: 'I am here.'

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — तीन वैदिक अग्नियों का तीन प्राणों से सम्बन्ध यह दिखाता है कि शरीर स्वयं एक यज्ञशाला (sacrificial arena) है। प्रत्येक श्वास एक आहुति है; प्रत्येक हृदय-स्पन्दन एक यज्ञ-क्रिया।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says mapping the three Vedic fires onto three prāṇas shows that the body itself is a sacrificial arena. Every breath is an oblation; every heartbeat is a ritual act.
aurobindo.ins: You don't need a fire-altar to perform sacrifice. Your body is the altar. The three fires burn in you day and night — apāna below, vyāna around, prāṇa above. Every breath is an offering. You've been performing yajña in your sleep.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the three Vedic fires?
dp.a: The treta-agni (triple fire) is the foundation of Vedic śrauta (solemn) ritual. Every initiated householder maintained these three fires: (1) Gārhapatya ('belonging to the householder') — the primary, perpetual fire kept in the western position. It is the 'source fire' from which the other two are kindled. It is never allowed to go out. It represents the domestic realm, the earth, and the root of life. → Mapped to apāna because apāna is the 'root' prāṇa — stationed in the lower body, governing the foundational functions (excretion, reproduction) that sustain the body's material base. (2) Anvāhāryapacana / Dakṣiṇāgni ('southern fire') — kindled from the Gārhapatya and placed in the southern position. It is used for cooking offerings and for ancestral rites. It represents the atmospheric realm and the intermediate zone. → Mapped to vyāna because vyāna pervades the entire body, just as this fire extends its influence across the ritual space. (3) Āhavanīya ('offering fire') — kindled from the Gārhapatya and placed in the eastern position. It is the fire into which all oblations are poured (the 'mouth' of the sacrifice). It represents the celestial realm. → Mapped to prāṇa (next mantra). The internalisation of these three fires as prāṇas is a radical Upanishadic move: it transforms every breathing body into a perpetual sacrifice — no priest, no altar, no ritual required.

dp.q: 🔍 Why do the prāṇas never sleep?
dp.a: The prāṇas (vital breaths) never cease during sleep because they sustain the body's involuntary functions — processes that must continue 24/7 for the organism to survive: Apāna (= Gārhapatya): continues excretory and reproductive processes during sleep — kidney filtration, intestinal peristalsis, cellular waste removal. If apāna stopped, toxins would accumulate fatally within hours. Vyāna (= Dakṣiṇāgni): continues blood circulation and nutrient distribution — the heart beats, blood flows, oxygen reaches cells. If vyāna stopped, tissues would die from oxygen deprivation within minutes. Prāṇa (= Āhavanīya, next mantra): continues respiration — breathing doesn't stop during sleep. If prāṇa stopped, death would follow within minutes. The Upanishadic insight is precise: the voluntary functions (seeing, hearing, speaking, grasping, walking) shut down during sleep — these are the ten indriyas. But the involuntary functions (breathing, heartbeat, digestion, circulation, elimination) continue — these are the prāṇas. The prāṇas are more fundamental than the senses because they sustain life itself, not just experience. You can live without sight or hearing; you cannot live without breath or heartbeat.

sk: यदुच्छ्वासनिःश्वासावेतावाहुती समं नयतीति स समानः मनो ह वाव यजमानो इष्टफलमेवोदानः स एनं यजमानमहरहर्ब्रह्म गमयति ||
ro: yat · ucchvāsa-niḥśvāsau · etau · āhutī · samaṁ · nayati · iti · saḥ · samānaḥ · manaḥ · ha · vāva · yajamānaḥ · iṣṭa-phalam · eva · udānaḥ · saḥ · enaṁ · yajamānam · ahar-ahaḥ · brahma · gamayati ||
hi: जो श्वास (ucchvāsa) और प्रश्वास (niḥśvāsa) — इन दो आहुतियों को समान रूप से (samaṁ) चलाता है — वह समान है। मन ही यजमान (sacrifice का कर्ता) है। इष्ट-फल (sacrifice का फल) — वह उदान है। वह (उदान) इस यजमान (मन) को प्रतिदिन (ahar-ahar) ब्रह्म तक ले जाता है।
en: That which leads these two oblations — inhalation (ucchvāsa) and exhalation (niḥśvāsa) — equally (sama), that is samāna. The mind (manas) is indeed the yajamāna (sacrificer). The fruit of the sacrifice (iṣṭa-phala) is udāna. It leads this sacrificer (the mind) to Brahman day after day (ahar-ahar).
gr: Completing the fire-metaphor: (continuing from mantra 3) Prāṇa = Āhavanīya fire (implied from the inhalation-exhalation as āhutis). Samāna = the priest who conducts the oblations equally. Mind = yajamāna (the patron-sacrificer). Udāna = iṣṭa-phala (the fruit of the sacrifice). The body-sacrifice: every breath-cycle is a complete sacrifice: inhalation and exhalation are two oblations (āhutī), samāna distributes them equally, the mind is the beneficiary, and udāna carries the mind to Brahman every night in deep sleep. ahar-ahar brahma gamayati — 'day after day, leads to Brahman': this is a striking claim — every night in deep sleep, the mind is led to Brahman. Deep sleep is a daily encounter with Brahman. Yet the sleeper returns without knowing it (because of avidyā). Liberation is making this nightly encounter conscious.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अहरहर्ब्रह्म गमयति' — प्रतिदिन सुषुप्ति (deep sleep) में मन ब्रह्म को स्पर्श करता है। यही कारण है कि सुषुप्ति से जागने पर सुख की अनुभूति होती है — ब्रह्म-सान्निध्य (proximity to Brahman) का प्रभाव। किन्तु अज्ञानी लौटकर भूल जाता है; ज्ञानी लौटकर जानता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ahar-ahar brahma gamayati' — every day in deep sleep, the mind touches Brahman. This is why we feel happy after waking from deep sleep — the effect of Brahman-proximity. But the ignorant person returns and forgets; the knower returns and knows.
advaita.ins: You visit Brahman every night. Every single night, in deep sleep, your mind dissolves into the Absolute. You come back refreshed, happy, renewed — because you were home. The tragedy is: you don't remember the visit. Liberation is remembering.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्म गमयति' — प्रतिदिन मन भगवान् के सान्निध्य में जाता है। सुषुप्ति = भगवान् की गोद में विश्राम। 'इष्टफल' = उदान भगवान् तक पहुँचाने वाला वाहन (vehicle) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'brahma gamayati' — daily the mind goes to the Lord's proximity. Deep sleep = resting in the Lord's lap. 'Iṣṭa-phala' = udāna is the vehicle that carries you to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Every night, udāna picks you up and carries you to God's lap. You rest there — in perfect safety, perfect peace. Then it brings you back. This is the Lord's daily gift to every creature. The devotee is the one who says: next time, let me stay.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अहरहर्ब्रह्म गमयति' — यह दैनिक 'समाधि' है — प्रत्येक सुषुप्ति में चेतना अपने स्रोत को स्पर्श करती है और नवीकृत (renewed) होकर लौटती है। यदि यह स्पर्श सचेतन (conscious) हो जाए, तो यही मुक्ति है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'ahar-ahar brahma gamayati' — this is a daily 'samādhi'. In every deep sleep, consciousness touches its source and returns renewed. If this touch becomes conscious, that is liberation.
aurobindo.ins: You practice samādhi every night without knowing it. Deep sleep is unconscious samādhi. The yogi's goal is to make it conscious — to stay awake while the mind dissolves into Brahman. Then sleep becomes liberation, and waking becomes play.

dp.q: 🔍 How is breathing a sacrifice?
dp.a: The Prashna Upanishad constructs a complete inner sacrifice (antaryāga) from the components of breathing: The three fires: Gārhapatya = apāna (root fire, lower body); Dakṣiṇāgni = vyāna (southern fire, pervading); Āhavanīya = prāṇa (offering fire, upper body). The two oblations: ucchvāsa (inhalation) and niḥśvāsa (exhalation). Each breath-cycle pours two offerings into the fire of life. The priest: samāna — the prāṇa that 'equalises', distributing the offerings evenly. The sacrificer: manas (the mind) — the patron who commissions and benefits from the sacrifice. The fruit: udāna — the upward-moving breath that carries the 'fruit' (the mind's connection to Brahman) to the sacrificer. This internalisation has revolutionary implications: (1) Every breathing being is performing a sacrifice — not just Vedic priests. (2) No external materials, altar, or ceremony are needed — the body is the altar. (3) The sacrifice never stops — it runs 24/7, even during sleep. (4) The 'fruit' is not worldly reward but Brahman itself — the mind is carried to Brahman every night.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'day after day to Brahman' mean?
dp.a: The phrase ahar-ahar brahma gamayati ('day after day, leads to Brahman') is one of the most remarkable statements in the Upanishads. It means: Every night, in deep sleep, the mind (yajamāna) is carried by udāna to Brahman. This claim has several implications: (1) Deep sleep = daily Brahman-contact: the happiness we feel after waking from dreamless sleep is not random — it is the afterglow of having been in Brahman's presence. The Chāndogya (6.8.1) says the same: 'When a man sleeps, he has merged with sat (Being).' (2) Why don't we know it? Because of avidyā (ignorance). In deep sleep, the mind merges with Brahman but is wrapped in ignorance — it cannot recognise what it has contacted. It is like a person who walks through a treasure-room blindfolded and comes out rich but unable to describe what he touched. (3) Liberation = conscious deep sleep: the yogi's goal is to enter the state of deep sleep with awareness intact — to experience the Brahman-contact knowingly. This is what the Māṇḍūkya calls turīya — the Fourth state, which has the bliss of deep sleep with the awareness of waking. (4) 'Day after day': this is not a one-time event but a daily occurrence. You go to Brahman every night. The question is not 'how do I get to Brahman?' but 'how do I recognise that I'm already going there?'

sk: अत्रैष देवः स्वप्ने महिमानमनुभवति यद्दृष्टं दृष्टमनुपश्यति श्रुतं श्रुतमेवार्थमनुशृणोति देशदिगन्तरैश्च प्रत्यनुभूतं पुनः पुनः प्रत्यनुभवति दृष्टं चादृष्टं च श्रुतं चाश्रुतं चानुभूतं चाननुभूतं च सच्चासच्च सर्वं पश्यति सर्वः पश्यति ||
ro: atra · eṣaḥ · devaḥ · svapne · mahimānam · anubhavati · yat · dṛṣṭaṁ · dṛṣṭam · anupaśyati · śrutaṁ · śrutam · eva · artham · anuśṛṇoti · deśa-dig-antaraiḥ · ca · pratyanubhūtaṁ · punaḥ · punaḥ · pratyanubhavati · dṛṣṭaṁ · ca · adṛṣṭaṁ · ca · śrutaṁ · ca · aśrutaṁ · ca · anubhūtaṁ · ca · ananubhūtaṁ · ca · sat · ca · asat · ca · sarvaṁ · paśyati · sarvaḥ · paśyati ||
hi: यहाँ (स्वप्न-अवस्था में) यह देव (मन) महिमा (greatness) का अनुभव करता है। जो (जागृति में) देखा गया — उसे फिर देखता है; जो सुना गया — उसे फिर सुनता है; विभिन्न देश-दिशाओं (स्थानों) में जो अनुभव किया गया — उसे बार-बार पुनः अनुभव करता है। दृष्ट (देखा) और अदृष्ट (न देखा), श्रुत (सुना) और अश्रुत (न सुना), अनुभूत (अनुभव किया) और अननुभूत (न अनुभव किया), सत् (विद्यमान) और असत् (अविद्यमान) — सब कुछ देखता है। सर्वः (सबकुछ होकर) देखता है।
en: Here (in the dream-state) this god (the mind) experiences its greatness (mahimāna). What was seen, it sees again; what was heard, it hears again; what was experienced in various places and directions, it experiences again and again. Seen and unseen, heard and unheard, experienced and unexperienced, existent and non-existent — it sees all. Being all (sarvaḥ), it sees.

ws.h: पुनः देखता है / अनुसरण करके देखता है
विभिन्न देश, दिशा और स्थानों में

gr: svapne mahimānam anubhavati — 'in dreams, it experiences its greatness': the mind's 'greatness' is that in dreams it becomes a creator. It constructs entire worlds — landscapes, people, events — from memory-traces (vāsanās), without any external input. No eye sees, no ear hears — yet the dreamer sees and hears. dṛṣṭaṁ ca adṛṣṭam ca... — six pairs of opposites: seen/unseen, heard/unheard, experienced/unexperienced, existent/non-existent. The dream-mind transcends all boundaries: it can see things never seen in waking, hear words never spoken, experience events that never happened. It creates from both memory (sat) and imagination (asat). sarvaḥ paśyati — 'being all, it sees': the most profound statement. In the dream, the mind is simultaneously (1) the seer, (2) the seen, and (3) the act of seeing. It is everything in the dream. This is used as a model for Brahman's creation: Brahman creates the waking world the way the mind creates the dream world — being everything, it 'sees' (manifests) everything.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'सर्वः पश्यति' — स्वप्न में मन सर्वरूप (everything) बन जाता है: द्रष्टा, दृश्य, और दर्शन-क्रिया — तीनों एक। यह ब्रह्म की सृष्टि का मॉडल (model) है — जैसे मन स्वप्न-जगत् बनाता है, वैसे ब्रह्म जाग्रत-जगत् बनाता है। दोनों जगत् मिथ्या (apparent) हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'sarvaḥ paśyati' — in dreams the mind becomes everything: seer, seen, and seeing are one. This is the model for Brahman's creation — as the mind creates the dream-world, so Brahman creates the waking-world. Both worlds are mithyā (apparent, not ultimately real).
advaita.ins: Last night you dreamt an entire world — mountains, rivers, people, conversations. You were the creator of that world, the experiencer of it, and the material it was made of. Now ask: what if waking is the same kind of thing? What if there's a dreamer who is dreaming this world — and that dreamer is you?

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'महिमानम्' — मन की यह सर्जन-शक्ति (creative power) ईश्वर की शक्ति का अंशमात्र (fraction) है। भगवान् जाग्रत-जगत् के सर्जक हैं; मन स्वप्न-जगत् का। अन्तर यह है कि भगवान् की सृष्टि स्वतंत्र (independent) है, मन की सृष्टि भगवान्-आश्रित (God-dependent) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'mahimāna' — the mind's creative power in dreams is a fraction of the Lord's power. The Lord creates the waking-world; the mind creates the dream-world. The difference: the Lord's creation is independent; the mind's creation is God-dependent.
vishisht.ins: In dreams, you're a mini-creator — you build worlds from nothing. But your creative power is borrowed. The Lord creates the waking world the same way, except His power is original. Your dream is a small echo of His grand creation.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — स्वप्न-अवस्था में चेतना अपनी आन्तरिक (inner/subliminal) शक्तियों को प्रकट करती है — बिना किसी बाह्य सहारे के सृजन करती है। 'सर्वः पश्यति' — यह अतिमानसिक (supramental) सृजन-शक्ति की झलक है — जहाँ द्रष्टा और दृश्य एक हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says in the dream-state, consciousness reveals its inner (subliminal) powers — creating without any external support. 'Sarvaḥ paśyati' — this is a glimpse of the supramental creative power where seer and seen are one.
aurobindo.ins: Dreams prove that consciousness doesn't need external matter to create a world. It can generate sight without eyes, sound without ears, space without extension. That's not a defect — it's a superpower. The Upanishad calls it mahimā — greatness.

dp.q: 🔍 The dream as a model for creation (svapna-dṛṣṭānta)
dp.a: The dream-analogy (svapna-dṛṣṭānta) is one of the most powerful arguments in Vedānta. The Prashna's statement 'sarvaḥ paśyati' ('being all, it sees') provides the basis: In the dream: (1) The mind creates a world without external matter. (2) The mind is simultaneously the creator, the material, and the experiencer of that world. (3) The dream-world appears completely real while dreaming — the dreamer doesn't doubt it. (4) On waking, the dreamer realises the dream-world was 'created' by the mind alone — it had no independent existence. The Vedāntic extension: Advaita Vedānta applies the same logic to the waking world: (1) Brahman creates the world without external matter (it is both the efficient and material cause). (2) Brahman is simultaneously the creator, the material, and the experiencer. (3) The waking world appears completely real while we're 'in' it. (4) On 'waking' to the truth (through jñāna), the seeker realises that the waking world too was 'projected' by Brahman — it has no independent existence apart from Brahman. This doesn't mean the world is 'unreal' (like a hallucination) — it means it is not independently real. It is real as a manifestation of Brahman, just as the dream is real as a manifestation of the mind. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.1.20) uses the spider-web analogy for the same purpose: 'As a spider sends forth its thread...'

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'sarvaḥ paśyati' (being all, it sees) mean?
dp.a: The phrase sarvaḥ paśyati is one of the most compressed metaphysical statements in the Upanishads. It means: the dreaming mind becomes the totality of the dream-world and, being everything, perceives everything. In ordinary waking perception, there is a triad: (1) the perceiver (draṣṭā), (2) the perceived (dṛśya), and (3) the act of perceiving (darśana). These appear distinct. In dreams, this triad collapses into one: the mind is simultaneously the eye that sees the dream-mountain, the mountain that is seen, and the seeing itself. There is no external mountain — the mind is the mountain. This collapse of the triad is philosophically decisive: If the subject-object distinction can collapse in dreams, it is not fundamental. It is not an irreducible feature of reality but a construct — something the mind can create and also dissolve. The Māṇḍūkya Upanishad builds its entire argument on this insight: if waking and dreaming share the same structure (a consciousness projecting a world and then experiencing it as 'other'), then waking is not categorically superior to dreaming — both are projections. The only state that is not a projection is turīya — the pure consciousness that is the source of all projections.

sk: स यदा तेजसाभिभूतो भवति अत्रैष देवः स्वप्नान्न पश्यत्यथ यदैतस्मिञ्शरीरे एतत्सुखं भवति ||
ro: saḥ · yadā · tejasā · abhibhūtaḥ · bhavati · atra · eṣaḥ · devaḥ · svapnān · na · paśyati · atha · yadā · etasmin · śarīre · etat · sukhaṁ · bhavati ||
hi: जब वह (मन-रूपी देव) तेज (प्रकाश/आत्म-ज्योति) से अभिभूत (overwhelmed/आच्छादित) हो जाता है — तब यह देव स्वप्न नहीं देखता। तब इस शरीर में यह सुख (आनन्द) होता है।
en: When he (the mind-god) becomes overwhelmed by light (tejas), then this god does not see dreams. Then in this body arises that happiness (sukha).
gr: tejasā abhibhūtaḥ — 'overwhelmed by light': a key phrase. What 'light' overwhelms the mind? The Ātman's own luminosity (svayam-prakāśa). In waking, the mind projects outward through the senses. In dreaming, it projects inward through memory-traces. In deep sleep, the projecting capacity itself is overwhelmed by the Ātman's radiance — like a candle flame overwhelmed by sunlight. The mind still exists (otherwise the person would be dead), but its projective function is suspended. svapnān na paśyati — 'does not see dreams': the transition from dream to deep sleep. Dreams cease not because the mind 'runs out' of material but because it is submerged in a greater light. etat sukhaṁ bhavati — 'this happiness arises': the happiness of deep sleep (suṣupti-sukha). This answers Sauryāyaṇī's fourth sub-question: 'Whose is this happiness?' It belongs to the Self (Ātman), and the mind experiences it by proximity — not by object-perception but by absorption.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'तेजसा अभिभूतः' — आत्मा के तेज (Self-luminosity) से मन की विक्षेप-शक्ति (projecting power) दब जाती है। सुषुप्ति में मन आत्मा में विलीन होता है — इसीलिए सुख होता है। यह सुख विषय-जन्य (object-caused) नहीं, आत्म-स्वरूप (Self-nature) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'tejasā abhibhūtaḥ' — the Self's luminosity suppresses the mind's projecting power. In deep sleep, the mind dissolves into the Ātman — hence the happiness. This happiness is not object-caused but is the Self's own nature (svarūpa-ānanda).
advaita.ins: In deep sleep, the mind's projector turns off. Not because it broke — but because the screen is flooded with a light so bright that no image can compete. That light is the Self. And that light is bliss.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'तेज' = भगवान् का प्रकाश। सुषुप्ति में जीव भगवान् के तेज में लीन हो जाता है — स्वप्न बन्द हो जाते हैं — और शेष रहता है केवल सुख (भगवत्-सान्निध्य का)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'tejas' = the Lord's light. In deep sleep, the jīva merges into the Lord's radiance — dreams cease — and only happiness remains (the proximity of the Lord).
vishisht.ins: Why is deep sleep happy? Because the Lord's light is so strong that the mind's movie-projector shuts down. What remains when the movie stops? The light itself. And the light is bliss.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'तेजसा अभिभूत' — सुषुप्ति में चेतना अपने अधिचेतन (superconscient) स्रोत से इतनी अधिक प्रकाशित होती है कि मानसिक स्तर (mental level) की गतिविधि अवरुद्ध हो जाती है। सुख = अधिचेतन आनन्द की झलक।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'tejasā abhibhūta' — in deep sleep, consciousness is so flooded by its superconscient source that mental-level activity is suppressed. The happiness = a glimpse of superconscient bliss.
aurobindo.ins: Deep sleep is like diving into the ocean of consciousness. The mind — a small torch — is overwhelmed by the ocean's luminosity. Dreams dissolve. What remains is the ocean's own nature: bliss. You surface every morning carrying drops of that ocean.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is deep sleep happy?
dp.a: The happiness of deep sleep (suṣupti-sukha) is one of the great mysteries explored in Vedānta. The Upanishadic answer is that deep-sleep happiness is the Self's own nature (svarūpa-ānanda), not caused by any external object: In waking, happiness comes from getting what you want — a meal, a promotion, a compliment. This is viṣayānanda (object-dependent happiness): it requires a subject, an object, and a contact between them. In deep sleep, there is no subject-object contact — yet happiness is present. This proves that happiness does not require an object. The Taittirīya Upanishad (2.7) confirms: 'This very being (the Self) is the source of bliss (raso vai saḥ).' The mechanism: in deep sleep, the mind's vikṣepa-śakti (projecting power) is 'overwhelmed' by the Ātman's light. Without projection, there is no desire, no frustration, no duality — just the Self resting in itself. This is its natural state: ānanda (bliss). Why don't we remember it? Because the mind's other power — āvaraṇa-śakti (concealing power) — remains active. The mind is near the Self but doesn't know it is. The veil of ignorance (avidyā) covers the recognition. This is why suṣupti is not liberation: in liberation, both powers (projection and concealment) cease. In suṣupti, only projection ceases — concealment remains.

dp.q: 🔍 The three states and their 'light-sources'
dp.a: Each state of consciousness has its own source of illumination: Waking (jāgrat): illuminated by external light — the sun, fire, lamps. The senses perceive objects lit by external sources. Without sunlight, the eye cannot see. Dream (svapna): illuminated by the mind's own light. In dreams, there is no external sun — yet the dreamer sees landscapes, faces, colours. The mind generates its own light (svayam-jyoti). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.3.9) asks: 'What light does the person have in the dream-state?' and answers: 'The mind itself is his light.' Deep sleep (suṣupti): illuminated by the Ātman's light — but this light is so overwhelming that the mind cannot process it. The mind is 'overwhelmed' (abhibhūta) — it cannot project images (dreams) because the background light is too bright. It's like trying to see stars during daytime: the stars are still there, but the sun's light makes them invisible. Turīya (the Fourth): the pure Ātman-light itself, without any mind to be overwhelmed. This is consciousness in its raw state — self-luminous, objectless, blissful, and fully aware. The progression: external light → mental light → overwhelming Self-light → pure Self-light. Each stage moves closer to the source of all illumination.

sk: स यथा सोम्य वयांसि वासोवृक्षं सम्प्रतिष्ठन्ते एवं ह वै तत्सर्वं पर आत्मनि सम्प्रतिष्ठते ||
ro: saḥ · yathā · somya · vayāṁsi · vāso-vṛkṣaṁ · sampratiṣṭhante · evaṁ · ha · vai · tat · sarvaṁ · pare · ātmani · sampratiṣṭhate ||
hi: हे सौम्य (प्रिय शिष्य)! जैसे पक्षी (वयांसि) अपने वास-वृक्ष (roosting tree / विश्राम-वृक्ष) पर जाकर बैठ जाते हैं — वैसे ही वह सब कुछ (सब इन्द्रियाँ, प्राण, मन) पर आत्मा (supreme Self) में प्रतिष्ठित हो जाता है।
en: As, O Somya (dear one), birds settle upon their roosting tree (vāso-vṛkṣa) — so all this settles in the supreme Self (para ātman).

ws.e: O dear one / O gentle one

ws.h: वास-वृक्ष / विश्राम-वृक्ष / जहाँ पक्षी रात बिताते हैं

gr: The bird-tree simile: one of the most tender images in the Upanishads. Birds scatter during the day to feed, explore, and sing. At dusk, they all return to one tree — their home. Similarly, the senses (birds) fly outward during waking, explore the world, and at night (sleep) return to their home — the Ātman (the roosting tree). somya — 'O dear one': the same term of endearment used by Uddālaka Āruṇi in the Chāndogya's great teaching 'tat tvam asi, somya' ('That thou art, dear one'). Its use here signals that Pippalāda is about to reveal the ultimate answer. pare ātmani sampratiṣṭhate — 'settles in the supreme Self': this answers Sauryāyaṇī's final sub-question: 'In whom are all established?' The answer: in the para ātman — the supreme Self. Not in the mind (which is itself a 'bird' that roosts), not in prāṇa, but in the Self which is the ground of all.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — पक्षी-वृक्ष उपमा यह दिखाती है कि सब कुछ — इन्द्रियाँ, मन, प्राण — अन्ततः आत्मा पर आश्रित (dependent) है। दिन में पक्षी उड़ते हैं (जागृति), रात में लौटते हैं (सुषुप्ति)। वृक्ष कभी नहीं हिलता — आत्मा कभी नहीं बदलता।
advaita.en: Shankara says the bird-tree simile shows everything — senses, mind, prāṇa — ultimately depends on the Ātman. During the day birds fly (waking), at night they return (deep sleep). The tree never moves — the Ātman never changes.
advaita.ins: All day your senses fly outward — seeing, hearing, touching, tasting. At night they all come home. Home is the Self — the one tree that never moves, never changes, never falls. You are not the birds. You are the tree.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'पर आत्मन' = परमात्मा (भगवान्)। सब जीव रात को (सुषुप्ति में) भगवान् में लौट जाते हैं — जैसे पक्षी अपने वृक्ष पर। यह भगवान् की शरणागति (surrender) का प्राकृतिक रूप है — निद्रा स्वतः शरणागति है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'para ātman' = Paramātman (the Lord). All beings return to the Lord in deep sleep — like birds to their tree. This is the natural form of surrender (śaraṇāgati) — sleep is automatic surrender.
vishisht.ins: Every night, without knowing it, you surrender to God. Your senses stop fighting, your mind stops planning, your ego stops claiming. You return to the tree. This is what devotion looks like when the ego isn't in the way.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — वास-वृक्ष (roosting tree) = चेतना का मूल (root of consciousness)। दिन में चेतना बहिर्मुख (outward-facing) होती है; रात में अन्तर्मुख (inward-facing)। दोनों दिशाओं का स्रोत एक — पर आत्मा।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the roosting tree = the root of consciousness. During the day, consciousness faces outward; at night, inward. The source of both directions is one — the supreme Self.
aurobindo.ins: The birds don't create the tree by roosting on it. The tree was there before the birds arrived, and it will be there after they leave. Similarly, the Self doesn't depend on the senses for its existence. It was there before perception began, and it remains when perception ceases.

dp.q: 🔍 The bird-tree simile and its meaning
dp.a: The bird-tree simile (vayāṁsi vāso-vṛkṣam) is one of the Prashna Upanishad's most original and beautiful images. Every evening, birds (vayāṁsi) that have scattered during the day to feed, explore, and sing return to their roosting tree (vāso-vṛkṣa) — the one place where they rest, sleep, and are safe. The correspondences: Birds = the senses, the mind, the prāṇas — all the faculties that 'fly outward' during waking. The tree = the supreme Self (para ātman) — the unchanging, unmoving ground to which everything returns. Day = waking — the senses spread outward, engaging with the world. Night = deep sleep — all faculties return to the Self. Key properties of the tree: (1) Stability: the tree doesn't move. The Self is immovable (acala), unchanging (avikāra). (2) Pre-existence: the tree existed before the birds arrived. The Self exists before the senses emerge. (3) Home: the tree is not just a stop — it is home. The Self is not just a temporary resting-place for the senses — it is their ultimate origin and destination. (4) Safety: birds roost in trees for protection from predators. The Self is the ultimate refuge — in deep sleep, there is no fear, no anxiety, no danger.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'para ātman' mean?
dp.a: The phrase para ātman (परम आत्मा, 'supreme Self') appears here as the answer to the question 'in whom are all established?' Its meaning varies across the three philosophical schools: Advaita: para ātman = nirguṇa Brahman, the attributeless Absolute. It is the one and only reality; the senses, mind, and prāṇas are its apparent manifestations (vivarta). In deep sleep, the apparent plurality dissolves back into the one Brahman. Vishishtadvaita: para ātman = Paramātman (Nārāyaṇa/Viṣṇu), the supreme Person who is distinct from yet inclusive of all individual selves (jīvātmans). The jīvas return to the Lord in deep sleep as birds return to the tree — they rest in Him but are not identical with Him. Aurobindo's Integral view: para ātman = the superconscient source of all consciousness. In deep sleep, the surface consciousness (which projects the waking and dream worlds) subsides, and the individual rests in the superconscient — the root-consciousness that is prior to all differentiation. Despite the philosophical differences, all three agree on the experiential point: in deep sleep, something real is contacted — a ground of happiness, safety, and renewal. That ground is the para ātman, however each school may define it.

sk: पृथिवी च पृथिवीमात्रा च आपश्चापोमात्रा च तेजश्च तेजोमात्रा च वायुश्च वायुमात्रा चाकाशश्चाकाशमात्रा च चक्षुश्च द्रष्टव्यं च श्रोत्रं च श्रोतव्यं च घ्राणं च घ्रातव्यं च रसश्च रसयितव्यं च त्वक्च स्पर्शयितव्यं च वाक्च वक्तव्यं च हस्तौ चादातव्यं चोपस्थश्चानन्दयितव्यं च पायुश्च विसर्जयितव्यं च पादौ च गन्तव्यं च मनश्च मन्तव्यं च बुद्धिश्च बोद्धव्यं चाहंकारश्चाहंकर्तव्यं च चित्तं च चेतयितव्यं च तेजश्च विद्योतयितव्यं च प्राणश्च विधारयितव्यं च ||
ro: pṛthivī · ca · pṛthivī-mātrā · ca · āpaḥ · ca · apo-mātrā · ca · tejaḥ · ca · tejo-mātrā · ca · vāyuḥ · ca · vāyu-mātrā · ca · ākāśaḥ · ca · ākāśa-mātrā · ca · cakṣuḥ · ca · draṣṭavyaṁ · ca · śrotraṁ · ca · śrotavyaṁ · ca · ghrāṇaṁ · ca · ghrātavyaṁ · ca · rasaḥ · ca · rasayitavyaṁ · ca · tvak · ca · sparśayitavyaṁ · ca · vāk · ca · vaktavyaṁ · ca · hastau · ca · ādātavyaṁ · ca · upasthaḥ · ca · ānandayitavyaṁ · ca · pāyuḥ · ca · visarjayitavyaṁ · ca · pādau · ca · gantavyaṁ · ca · manaḥ · ca · mantavyaṁ · ca · buddhiḥ · ca · boddhavyaṁ · ca · ahaṁkāraḥ · ca · ahaṁkartavyaṁ · ca · cittaṁ · ca · cetayitavyaṁ · ca · tejaḥ · ca · vidyotayitavyaṁ · ca · prāṇaḥ · ca · vidhārayitavyaṁ · ca ||
hi: पृथ्वी और पृथ्वी-मात्रा (सूक्ष्म तत्त्व), जल और जल-मात्रा, तेज और तेज-मात्रा, वायु और वायु-मात्रा, आकाश और आकाश-मात्रा; चक्षु और दृष्टव्य (देखने योग्य), श्रोत्र और श्रोतव्य (सुनने योग्य), घ्राण और घ्रातव्य (सूँघने योग्य), रस (जिह्वा) और रसयितव्य (चखने योग्य), त्वक् और स्पर्शयितव्य (छूने योग्य); वाक् और वक्तव्य (बोलने योग्य), हस्त और आदातव्य (ग्रहण योग्य), उपस्थ और आनन्दयितव्य (आनन्द योग्य), पायु और विसर्जयितव्य (त्यागने योग्य), पाद और गन्तव्य (जाने योग्य); मन और मन्तव्य (विचारणीय), बुद्धि और बोद्धव्य (जानने योग्य), अहंकार और अहंकर्तव्य (अहंकार-कर्तव्य), चित्त और चेतयितव्य (चेतना-योग्य); तेज और विद्योतयितव्य (प्रकाशित करने योग्य), प्राण और विधारयितव्य (धारण करने योग्य) — (ये सब पर आत्मा में प्रतिष्ठित हैं)।
en: Earth and earth-essence (tanmātra), water and water-essence, fire and fire-essence, air and air-essence, space and space-essence; the eye and what is to be seen, the ear and what is to be heard, the nose and what is to be smelled, taste and what is to be tasted, skin and what is to be touched; speech and what is to be spoken, hands and what is to be grasped, the reproductive organ and what is to be enjoyed, the excretory organ and what is to be discharged, feet and what is to be walked; mind and what is to be thought, intellect and what is to be known, ego and what is to be ego-ised, memory and what is to be cognised; light and what is to be illuminated, prāṇa and what is to be sustained — (all these are established in the supreme Self).
gr: This mantra is a comprehensive enumeration of everything that 'settles' in the Ātman — continuing from mantra 7's bird-tree simile. The list covers: Five mahābhūtas + five tanmātras (10): earth/earth-essence, water/water-essence, fire/fire-essence, air/air-essence, space/space-essence. Five jñānendriyas + five viṣayas (10): eye/visible, ear/audible, nose/smellable, tongue/tastable, skin/touchable. Five karmendriyas + five functions (10): speech/speakable, hands/graspable, genitals/enjoyable, anus/dischargeable, feet/walkable. Four antaḥkaraṇa + four functions (8): mind/thinkable, intellect/knowable, ego/ego-able, memory/cognisable. Tejas + illuminable, Prāṇa + sustainble (4). Total: 42 items (21 pairs). This exhaustive list establishes that absolutely everything — gross and subtle, material and mental, active and passive — depends on the Ātman. Nothing has independent existence.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 21 युग्मों (pairs) की यह गणना सिद्ध करती है कि द्रष्टा (perceiver) और दृश्य (perceived) — दोनों आत्मा पर आश्रित हैं। इसलिए जगत् और जीव — दोनों ब्रह्म के विवर्त (apparent modifications) हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says the enumeration of 21 pairs proves that both perceiver and perceived depend on the Ātman. Therefore both the world and the individual are vivarta (apparent modifications) of Brahman.
advaita.ins: Everything comes in pairs — the seer and the seen, the thinker and the thought, the breather and the breathed. But every pair rests on one tree. The tree is not one of the pairs — it's the ground they all share.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — ये 42 तत्त्व भगवान् के शरीर (body of God) हैं। प्रत्येक तत्त्व भगवान् की विभूति (glory) है — कोई भी स्वतंत्र नहीं, सब ईश्वराश्रित (God-dependent) हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says these 42 principles are the body (śarīra) of God. Each principle is a vibhūti (glory) of the Lord — none is independent, all are God-dependent.
vishisht.ins: 42 principles, zero independent ones. Every element, every sense, every thought depends on the Lord. It's not a universe of parts — it's one body with 42 departments.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — यह सूची चेतना की सम्पूर्ण संरचना (complete architecture of consciousness) है — भौतिक (material) से लेकर प्राणिक (vital) से लेकर मानसिक (mental) तक। सब कुछ एक मूल चेतना (para ātman) में प्रतिष्ठित है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says this list is the complete architecture of consciousness — from material to vital to mental. Everything is established in one root-consciousness (para ātman).
aurobindo.ins: From the densest earth to the subtlest thought, from the grossest sense to the finest intuition — every level of reality is a branch of one tree. The tree is consciousness. Pull up the tree, and every branch, leaf, and fruit vanishes.

dp.q: 🔍 Why list everything in pairs?
dp.a: The mantra lists 21 pairs, each consisting of a faculty (the perceiver/actor) and its object (what it perceives/acts upon). Examples: eye + visible, ear + audible, mind + thinkable. The pairing is philosophically significant: (1) Both sides of experience depend on the Ātman: not just the subject (the seer) but also the object (the seen) rests in the Self. This rules out both naive realism ('the world exists independently of consciousness') and naive idealism ('only the mind exists; the world is pure illusion'). Both subject and object arise from the Self. (2) The pairs model the subject-object structure of all experience: every experience has a perceiver and a perceived. By showing that all such pairs rest in the Ātman, the Upanishad argues that the subject-object structure itself is dependent — it is not fundamental reality but a structure that emerges from the Self. (3) In deep sleep, all pairs dissolve: the eye and the visible, the ear and the audible — all merge back into the Ātman. This dissolution is the 'return of the birds to the tree.' When the pairs re-emerge (on waking), they re-emerge from the Ātman. The Self is both their source and their resting-place.

dp.q: 🔍 The four-fold inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa)
dp.a: The mantra lists four internal faculties — manas, buddhi, ahaṁkāra, citta — collectively called the antaḥkaraṇa (inner instrument) in Vedānta: (1) Manas (mind): deliberates, doubts, considers options. 'Should I do this or that?' Function: saṅkalpa-vikalpa (resolution and doubt). (2) Buddhi (intellect): decides, discriminates, determines. 'This is right; that is wrong.' Function: niścaya (determination). Buddhi is 'higher' than manas because it resolves what manas merely debates. (3) Ahaṁkāra (ego): claims ownership and agency. 'I see. I think. I do.' Function: abhimāna (self-identification). Without ahaṁkāra, there would be perception but no 'perceiver' who claims the perception as his own. (4) Citta (memory/consciousness-field): stores impressions (saṁskāras), enables recall, and maintains the continuity of personal identity. Function: smaraṇa (remembrance). These four are not four separate organs but four functions of one inner instrument — like four tools on a Swiss army knife. Together, they constitute the sūkṣma-śarīra (subtle body) that persists across births. In deep sleep, all four merge into the Ātman; on waking, they re-emerge with their accumulated impressions intact.

sk: एष हि द्रष्टा स्प्रष्टा श्रोता घ्राता रसयिता मन्ता बोद्धा कर्ता विज्ञानात्मा पुरुषः स परे ऽक्षर आत्मनि सम्प्रतिष्ठते ||
ro: eṣaḥ · hi · draṣṭā · spraṣṭā · śrotā · ghrātā · rasayitā · mantā · boddhā · kartā · vijñāna-ātmā · puruṣaḥ · saḥ · pare · akṣare · ātmani · sampratiṣṭhate ||
hi: यह (जीव/पुरुष) ही द्रष्टा (देखने वाला), स्प्रष्टा (स्पर्श करने वाला), श्रोता (सुनने वाला), घ्राता (सूँघने वाला), रसयिता (स्वाद लेने वाला), मन्ता (विचार करने वाला), बोद्धा (जानने वाला), कर्ता (करने वाला) है — (यह) विज्ञानात्मा पुरुष (ज्ञान-स्वरूप आत्मा) है। वह पर अक्षर आत्मा (अविनाशी परम आत्मा) में प्रतिष्ठित है।
en: This indeed is the seer (draṣṭā), toucher, hearer, smeller, taster, thinker, knower, doer — the person whose self is consciousness (vijñāna-ātmā puruṣa). He is established in the supreme, imperishable Self (para akṣara ātman).

ws.e: the self that is consciousness / the knowing self

ws.h: कर्ता / करने वाला / क्रिया करने वाला

gr: Eight agent-nouns: draṣṭā (seer), spraṣṭā (toucher), śrotā (hearer), ghrātā (smeller), rasayitā (taster), mantā (thinker), boddhā (knower), kartā (doer). These eight cover the entire range of subjective experience. vijñāna-ātmā puruṣaḥ — 'the person whose self is consciousness': this is the jīvātman — the individual self that acts as the agent of all perception and action. It is not merely a body or a mind but a consciousness (vijñāna) that animates both. pare akṣare ātmani sampratiṣṭhate — 'is established in the supreme, imperishable Self': the crucial climax. The vijñāna-ātmā (individual conscious self) is not self-grounding — it rests on the akṣara (imperishable) Ātman. This introduces a two-tier model: (1) the individual self (vijñāna-ātmā) who perceives and acts; (2) the supreme Self (para akṣara ātman) in whom the individual is established. The relationship between these two is the central question of all Vedānta.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'विज्ञानात्मा पुरुषः' = जीवात्मा — जो अविद्या-वशात् द्रष्टा, श्रोता आदि बना है। 'पर अक्षर आत्मा' = ब्रह्म — जो नित्य, अविनाशी, निर्गुण है। जीवात्मा ब्रह्म में प्रतिष्ठित है — अर्थात् जीव और ब्रह्म अन्ततः एक हैं; भेद अविद्या-कृत है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'vijñāna-ātmā puruṣa' = the jīvātman, who becomes seer, hearer, etc. through avidyā. 'Para akṣara ātman' = Brahman — eternal, imperishable, attributeless. The jīvātman is 'established' in Brahman — meaning they are ultimately one; the difference is avidyā-created.
advaita.ins: The seer, the hearer, the thinker, the doer — that's who you think you are. But this 'you' is grounded in something imperishable that doesn't see, hear, think, or do. It simply is. Your whole active life rests on an inactive ground — and that ground is the real you.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'विज्ञानात्मा' = जीवात्मा — भगवान् का अंश (part)। 'पर अक्षर आत्मा' = परमात्मा। जीव परमात्मा में प्रतिष्ठित है — जैसे शरीर आत्मा में। जीव भगवान् का शरीर है; भगवान् जीव की आत्मा हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'vijñāna-ātmā' = jīvātman, a part (aṁśa) of the Lord. 'Para akṣara ātman' = Paramātman. The jīva is established in Paramātman as the body is in the soul. The jīva is God's body; God is the jīva's soul.
vishisht.ins: You are the body of God. God is your soul. The seer, hearer, thinker — that's you, the body. But you are grounded in a soul you can't see: the imperishable Lord. You function because He exists. He doesn't function because you do.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'विज्ञानात्मा' = व्यक्तिगत चेतना (individual consciousness) जो विभिन्न भूमिकाओं (roles) में अभिनय करती है — द्रष्टा, श्रोता, कर्ता आदि। 'पर अक्षर आत्मा' = सच्चिदानन्द (सत्-चित्-आनन्द) — अविनाशी ब्रह्म जो सब व्यक्तिगत चेतनाओं का स्रोत है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'vijñāna-ātmā' = the individual consciousness that plays various roles — seer, hearer, doer, etc. 'Para akṣara ātman' = Satchidananda (Existence-Consciousness-Bliss) — the imperishable Brahman that is the source of all individual consciousnesses.
aurobindo.ins: You play eight roles — seer, hearer, thinker, doer, and more. But the actor is not the roles. Behind every role is a consciousness that doesn't change when the role changes. That consciousness rests in the imperishable. Find the actor behind the roles, and you've found the immortal.

dp.q: 🔍 Vijñāna-ātmā and akṣara ātman: the two-tier Self
dp.a: This mantra introduces a two-tier model of the Self: Tier 1: Vijñāna-ātmā (the consciousness-self) — the individual who perceives, thinks, and acts. It is the 'agent' (kartā) behind all eight functions listed: seeing, touching, hearing, smelling, tasting, thinking, knowing, doing. In Sāṅkhya terms, this is the puruṣa as witness; in Vedāntic terms, it is the jīvātman (individual self). Tier 2: Para akṣara ātman (the supreme imperishable Self) — the ground in which the vijñāna-ātmā is established. This is Brahman — the unchanging, undecaying reality that underlies all individual existence. The relationship between the two tiers is the central debate of Indian philosophy: Advaita: they are identical — the vijñāna-ātmā is the akṣara ātman, appearing as an individual only due to avidyā (ignorance). Realisation = recognising the identity. Vishishtadvaita: they are distinct but inseparable — the vijñāna-ātmā is a real part of the akṣara ātman, related as body to soul. The part can never become the whole, but it can know the whole through devotion. Dvaita: they are eternally distinct — the individual self is real and permanently different from the supreme Self. The Prashna Upanishad's wording — 'sampratiṣṭhate' (is established in) — is open to all three interpretations. It says the individual rests in the supreme — without specifying whether 'resting in' means identity, inherence, or dependence.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'akṣara' (imperishable) mean?
dp.a: The word akṣara (अक्षर) is one of the most significant terms in the Upanishads and the Gītā. Etymologically: a (not) + kṣara (perishable, from √kṣar, to flow away/decay) = 'that which does not perish, does not decay, does not flow away.' The term appears in: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.8-11: Gārgī asks Yājñavalkya: 'What is that akṣara in which space itself is woven?' Yājñavalkya answers: 'It is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long... It is the seer but is not seen, the hearer but is not heard, the thinker but is not thought, the knower but is not known. There is nothing other than it that sees, hears, thinks, or knows. In this akṣara, Gārgī, space is woven.' Bhagavad Gītā 8.3: 'Akṣaraṁ brahma paramam' — 'The imperishable is the supreme Brahman.' Gītā 15.16-18: 'There are two puruṣas in the world — kṣara (perishable) and akṣara (imperishable). All beings are kṣara; the unchanging is akṣara. But there is another, the Puruṣottama (supreme Person), who pervades and sustains the three worlds.' In the Prashna's usage, para akṣara ātman = the supreme imperishable Self — the final answer to 'in whom are all established?' Everything — elements, senses, mind, ego, prāṇa — rests in this imperishable ground. It never decays, never changes, never dies. It is the roosting tree that outlasts every bird.

sk: परमेवाक्षरं प्रतिपद्यते स यो ह वै तदच्छायमशरीरमलोहितं शुभ्रमक्षरं वेदयते यस्तु सोम्य स सर्वज्ञः सर्वो भवति तदेष श्लोकः ||
ro: param · eva · akṣaraṁ · pratipadyate · saḥ · yaḥ · ha · vai · tat · acchāyam · aśarīraṁ · alohitam · śubhram · akṣaraṁ · vedayate · yaḥ · tu · somya · saḥ · sarvajñaḥ · sarvaḥ · bhavati · tat · eṣaḥ · ślokaḥ ||
hi: वह परम अक्षर (अविनाशी ब्रह्म) को प्रतिपद्यते (प्राप्त करता है) — जो उस छायारहित (acchāya), शरीररहित (aśarīra), रक्तहीन (alohita), शुभ्र (luminous/pure), अक्षर (अविनाशी) को जानता है (vedayate)। हे सौम्य! वह सर्वज्ञ (omniscient) और सर्व (everything) हो जाता है। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: He attains (pratipadyate) the supreme imperishable (akṣara) — he who knows that shadowless (acchāya), bodiless (aśarīra), bloodless (alohita), pure/luminous (śubhra), imperishable (akṣara) (Brahman). O Somya! He becomes omniscient (sarvajña) and becomes all (sarva). On this there is this verse —
gr: Five via-negativa descriptions: acchāya (shadowless), aśarīra (bodiless), alohita (bloodless), śubhra (pure/luminous), akṣara (imperishable). The first three are negations — what Brahman is not. The last two are affirmations — what Brahman is: pure and imperishable. This is the Upanishadic neti-neti (not this, not this) method: define the Absolute by removing all limitations. sarvajñaḥ sarvaḥ bhavati — 'becomes omniscient and becomes all': the two-fold fruit of knowing akṣara. Sarvajña (omniscient) because the ground of all knowledge is known; sarva (all) because the ground of all being is known. Compare Muṇḍaka 3.2.9: 'sa yo ha vai tat paramaṁ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati' — 'he who knows that supreme Brahman, becomes Brahman indeed.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — पाँच विशेषण (acchāya, aśarīra, alohita, śubhra, akṣara) निर्गुण ब्रह्म (attributeless Brahman) की ओर संकेत करते हैं। 'सर्वज्ञ सर्व भवति' — ब्रह्म-ज्ञानी ब्रह्म ही हो जाता है — यह जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation while alive) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the five adjectives (shadowless, bodiless, bloodless, pure, imperishable) point to nirguṇa Brahman (attributeless Brahman). 'Sarvajña sarva bhavati' — the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman — this is jīvanmukti (liberation while alive).
advaita.ins: No shadow — because there's no body to cast one. No body — because it's not a thing. No blood — because it's not alive in the way a creature is alive. What's left? Pure light. Imperishable. Know that, and you become that. There is nothing else to become.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अक्षर' = भगवान् का दिव्य शरीर (divine body) — जो प्राकृत शरीर (material body) से सर्वथा भिन्न है। 'सर्वज्ञ सर्व भवति' — भक्त भगवत्-ज्ञान प्राप्त कर भगवान् के स्वरूप (nature) को जान लेता है — 'सर्व' = भगवान् के गुणों (attributes) से सम्पन्न।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'akṣara' = the Lord's divine body — completely different from a material body. 'Sarvajña sarva bhavati' — the devotee, gaining knowledge of the Lord, knows the Lord's nature — 'sarva' = endowed with the Lord's attributes.
vishisht.ins: Shadowless, bodiless, bloodless — but not nothing. Pure, imperishable — this is the Lord's divine form. Know it, and you know everything. Not because you memorise the universe, but because you know the one thing everything is made of.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अच्छाय, अशरीर, अलोहित, शुभ्र, अक्षर' — ये सच्चिदानन्द (Existence-Consciousness-Bliss) के लक्षण हैं — पदार्थ (matter) से परे, रूप (form) से परे, किन्तु शून्य (void) नहीं — शुभ्र (luminous) = सत्-चेतना का स्वयं-प्रकाश।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'shadowless, bodiless, bloodless, pure, imperishable' are characteristics of Satchidananda — beyond matter, beyond form, but not void. Śubhra (luminous) = the self-luminosity of Truth-Consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The Absolute is not darkness. It is not void. It is not emptiness. It is light — so pure it has no shadow, so subtle it has no body, so alive it needs no blood. It is the one thing that never dies. Know it, and you know everything — because everything is made of it.

dp.q: 🔍 The via negativa (neti-neti) description of Brahman
dp.a: The five adjectives — acchāya, aśarīra, alohita, śubhra, akṣara — employ the classic Upanishadic neti-neti ('not this, not this') method of describing the Absolute: Acchāya (shadowless): a shadow requires a body and a light-source. Brahman has neither — it is the light and has no form to cast a shadow. Aśarīra (bodiless): Brahman has no gross body (sthūla-śarīra), no subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra), and no causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra). It transcends all three levels of embodiment. Alohita (bloodless): this specifically negates material life. Blood is the signature of biological embodiment — Brahman has no biological constitution. Śubhra (pure/luminous): the first positive description. After stripping away shadow, body, and blood, what remains is not nothing but pure light — the self-luminous consciousness (svayam-prakāśa). Akṣara (imperishable): the second positive description. Brahman never decays, changes, or dies. It is the one reality that outlasts every cycle of creation and dissolution. The method: first negate everything finite (acchāya, aśarīra, alohita). Then affirm what survives the negation (śubhra, akṣara). What you cannot negate — pure luminous imperishable consciousness — is Brahman. This method appears across the Upanishads: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.8 (the akṣara is 'neither this nor that'), Māṇḍūkya 7 (turīya is 'not conscious, not unconscious... ungraspable, without feature'), and Gītā 13.12 ('neither sat nor asat is it said to be').

dp.q: 🔍 'He becomes all' — what does this mean?
dp.a: The declaration 'sarvajñaḥ sarvaḥ bhavati' ('he becomes omniscient and becomes all') is one of the boldest claims in the Upanishads. It appears repeatedly: Muṇḍaka 3.2.9, Chāndogya 7.25.2, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10. What does 'becoming all' mean? Advaita reading: the individual was always Brahman — the 'becoming' is not a change but a recognition. When ignorance (avidyā) is removed, the jīva recognises that it was Brahman all along. 'Becoming all' = realising 'I was always all.' Vishishtadvaita reading: the devotee doesn't literally become God but attains God-like qualities (omniscience, etc.) in the liberated state. He becomes 'sarva' in the sense of participating in the Lord's nature — as a drop participates in the ocean. Aurobindo's reading: the individual consciousness expands to embrace the universal. It doesn't lose its individuality but contains the universal within it — like a hologram where each part contains the whole. The practical consequence, all schools agree: the knower of Brahman no longer fears. Fear comes from a sense of otherness ('there is something other than me that can harm me'). When you know you are all, there is no 'other' to fear. This is why the Taittirīya (2.7) says: 'When one finds fearlessness (abhaya) in that invisible, bodiless, indefinable, supportless — then one has reached fearlessness.'

sk: विज्ञानात्मा सह देवैश्च सर्वैः प्राणा भूतानि सम्प्रतिष्ठन्ति यत्र तदक्षरं वेदयते यस्तु सोम्य स सर्वज्ञः सर्वमेवाविवेशेति ||
ro: vijñāna-ātmā · saha · devaiḥ · ca · sarvaiḥ · prāṇāḥ · bhūtāni · sampratiṣṭhanti · yatra · tat · akṣaraṁ · vedayate · yaḥ · tu · somya · saḥ · sarvajñaḥ · sarvam · eva · āviveśa · iti ||
hi: विज्ञानात्मा (ज्ञान-स्वरूप जीव) समस्त देवों (शक्तियों) सहित, सब प्राण और सब भूत (तत्त्व/प्राणी) — जहाँ (जिसमें) प्रतिष्ठित होते हैं — जो उस अक्षर (अविनाशी ब्रह्म) को जानता है, हे सौम्य! वह सर्वज्ञ (omniscient) हो जाता है — वह सर्व (सब कुछ) में प्रविष्ट हो जाता है (आविवेश)। — इति (इस प्रकार चौथा प्रश्न समाप्त)।
en: The consciousness-self (vijñāna-ātmā), together with all the gods, the prāṇas, and the elements — where (yatra) all these are established — he who knows that imperishable (akṣara), O Somya, he becomes omniscient (sarvajña) and enters into all (sarvam āviveśa). — Thus (ends the fourth question).

ws.h: प्रविष्ट हो गया / सब में घुस गया

gr: The concluding verse repeats and amplifies the promise of mantra 10. The structure: (1) vijñāna-ātmā + devāḥ + prāṇāḥ + bhūtāni — the entire manifest reality; (2) yatra sampratiṣṭhanti — where all this is established; (3) tat akṣaraṁ vedayate — he who knows that imperishable; (4) sarvajñaḥ sarvam āviveśa — he becomes omniscient and enters all. sarvam āviveśa — 'entered into all': this is stronger than 'becomes all' (mantra 10). It means the knower pervades all of reality — not by physical expansion but by the realisation that there is no boundary between self and world. The Isha Upanishad (6) says the same: 'He who sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings — he never turns away.' iti — the formal close of Question 4. The teaching on the three states of consciousness is complete.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'सर्वमेवाविवेश' — ज्ञानी सब में प्रवेश कर गया — अर्थात् उसे ज्ञात हो गया कि 'मैं ही सब हूँ; सब कुछ मेरी ही अभिव्यक्ति है।' यही ब्रह्मानुभव (Brahman-experience) है — यही मोक्ष है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'sarvam āviveśa' — the knower has 'entered all' — meaning he has realised 'I am all; everything is my own manifestation.' This is the Brahman-experience — this is mokṣa.
advaita.ins: The knower doesn't travel anywhere. He simply opens his eyes — and sees himself in everything. The bird, the tree, the sun, the earth, the breath, the silence between breaths. Everything is himself. He has entered all — because he was always all.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सर्वमाविवेश' — भक्त भगवान् के सर्वव्यापी स्वरूप (all-pervading nature) को जानकर सब में भगवान् को देखता है — 'वासुदेवः सर्वम्' (गीता 7.19) — सब कुछ वासुदेव (भगवान्) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'sarvam āviveśa' — the devotee, knowing the Lord's all-pervading nature, sees the Lord in everything — 'vāsudevaḥ sarvam' (Gītā 7.19) — everything is Vāsudeva (the Lord).
vishisht.ins: The devotee doesn't become God. He sees God everywhere. In every face, every element, every breath — Vāsudeva. This is not pantheism — it's the result of knowing the one Lord who pervades all things. You haven't become all. You've recognised the One who is all.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'सर्वमाविवेश' — चेतना अपनी सीमाओं (boundaries) को तोड़कर सार्वभौमिक (universal) हो जाती है। व्यक्तिगत चेतना (individual consciousness) ब्रह्माण्डीय चेतना (cosmic consciousness) में विस्तृत होती है — किन्तु व्यक्तित्व (individuality) नष्ट नहीं होता, वह विशालतर (enlarged) हो जाता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'sarvam āviveśa' — consciousness breaks its boundaries and becomes universal. Individual consciousness expands into cosmic consciousness — but individuality is not destroyed, it is enlarged.
aurobindo.ins: You don't dissolve into the cosmos like salt into water. You expand to contain the cosmos — like the sky containing all the clouds. Individuality doesn't end — it becomes big enough to hold everything. That's what 'entering all' means.

dp.q: 🔍 Summary of Question 4's teaching
dp.a: Question 4 covers the three states of consciousness and the ground on which they rest: Mantra 1: Five sub-questions — what sleeps, what wakes, who dreams, whose is the happiness, in whom are all established? Mantra 2: Sleep: the sun-ray simile — all ten senses merge into the mind (para deva). Ten negations define the sleep state. Mantras 3-4: What stays awake: the prāṇa-fires (mapped to the three Vedic fires: Gārhapatya = apāna, Dakṣiṇāgni = vyāna, Āhavanīya = prāṇa). Breathing = sacrifice; mind = sacrificer; udāna carries the mind to Brahman every night. Mantra 5: Dreams: the mind experiences its 'greatness' (mahimā) — it creates an entire world from memory. 'Sarvaḥ paśyati' — being all, it sees. Mantra 6: Deep sleep: the mind is overwhelmed by the Ātman's light (tejasā abhibhūtaḥ). Dreams cease. Objectless happiness (sukha) arises. Mantra 7: Ground: the bird-tree simile — all faculties roost in the supreme Self (para ātman). Mantra 8: The 42-item enumeration — everything that 'roosts' in the Self. Mantras 9-11: The vijñāna-ātmā (consciousness-self) rests in the para akṣara ātman (supreme imperishable Self). The knower of this becomes omniscient and 'enters all.'

dp.q: 🔍 How does Question 4 relate to the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad?
dp.a: Question 4 of the Prashna and the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad cover the same territory — the three states of consciousness — but with different emphases: Shared content: Both analyse waking (jāgrat), dreaming (svapna), and deep sleep (suṣupti). Both identify a ground-state beyond all three. Both connect deep sleep with happiness and proximity to Brahman. Differences: The Māṇḍūkya (12 mantras + Gauḍapāda's Kārikā) is a systematic treatise: it names the Self in each state (Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña), identifies the Fourth (Turīya) explicitly, and maps all four to the syllable OM (A-U-M + silence). The Prashna's treatment is more narrative and metaphorical: it uses the sun-ray simile, the three-fires metaphor, the bird-tree image, and the 42-item enumeration. It doesn't name the states formally or map them to OM (that comes in Question 5). Complementary: the Prashna prepares the ground for the Māṇḍūkya's analysis. It establishes: (1) sleep = sense-withdrawal into mind; (2) dreams = mind's creative projection; (3) deep sleep = mind overwhelmed by Ātman's light; (4) all states rest in the akṣara (imperishable Self). The Māṇḍūkya then takes these insights and distils them into a single-syllable meditation: OM. Together, the two Upanishads form a complete consciousness-theory — the Prashna as narrative exposition, the Māṇḍūkya as systematic formula.
